## Proof

**The statement is TRUE for all positive integers \(n\).**

We prove that for every positive integer \(n\) and every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exist primes \(p, q\) with \(\left|\frac{p}{q} - n\right| < \varepsilon\).

---

**Case 1: \(\varepsilon \geq n\).**

Take \(p = q = 2\). Then
$$\left|\frac{p}{q} - n\right| = |1 - n| = n - 1 < n \leq \varepsilon. \quad\checkmark$$

---

**Case 2: \(0 < \varepsilon < n\).**

We use the **Prime Number Theorem** (PNT): \(\pi(x) \sim \frac{x}{\ln x}\) as \(x \to \infty\).

For a (large) prime \(q\), consider the open interval
$$I_q = \bigl((n-\varepsilon)\,q,\;(n+\varepsilon)\,q\bigr).$$
Since \(\varepsilon < n\), we have \(n - \varepsilon > 0\), so \(I_q\) lies entirely in the positive reals. Its length is \(2\varepsilon q > 0\).

The number of primes in \(I_q\) is
$$\pi\bigl((n+\varepsilon)q\bigr) - \pi\bigl((n-\varepsilon)q\bigr).$$

By PNT, as \(q \to \infty\):
$$\pi\bigl((n+\varepsilon)q\bigr) \sim \frac{(n+\varepsilon)\,q}{\ln\bigl((n+\varepsilon)q\bigr)}, \qquad \pi\bigl((n-\varepsilon)q\bigr) \sim \frac{(n-\varepsilon)\,q}{\ln\bigl((n-\varepsilon)q\bigr)}.$$

Since \(\ln\bigl((n\pm\varepsilon)q\bigr) = \ln q + \ln(n\pm\varepsilon) \sim \ln q\) as \(q \to \infty\), we obtain
$$\pi\bigl((n+\varepsilon)q\bigr) - \pi\bigl((n-\varepsilon)q\bigr) \;\sim\; \frac{(n+\varepsilon)q - (n-\varepsilon)q}{\ln q} = \frac{2\varepsilon\, q}{\ln q} \;\xrightarrow{q\to\infty}\; \infty.$$

Hence for all sufficiently large \(q\), the interval \(I_q\) contains at least one prime \(p\).

Since there are infinitely many primes, we may **choose \(q\) to be a prime exceeding this threshold**. Then \(p \in I_q\) gives
$$(n-\varepsilon)\,q < p < (n+\varepsilon)\,q \implies \left|\frac{p}{q} - n\right| < \varepsilon. \quad\checkmark$$

---

Both cases yield primes \(p, q\) with \(\left|\frac{p}{q} - n\right| < \varepsilon\). Therefore the statement holds for every positive integer \(n\). $\blacksquare$
